title: LS Lowry was weirder than you think
gist: Art critic David McAllister reviews MK Gallery's 'Lowry: The Theatre of Life', arguing that 50 years after his death LS Lowry was a trained, impressionist-influenced, deliberately unreal and eccentric painter rather than the naive working-class chronicler of popular myth.

insights.claim: Fifty years after his death, LS Lowry's popular image as an outsider, self-taught, working-class painter is wrong: he trained for a decade in evening classes, was an able draughtsman and absorbed continental impressionist influence.
insights.speaker: David McAllister
insights.so_what: Reappraisal exhibitions can reposition an artist's critical standing and, by extension, secondary-market interest in their work.
insights.quote: He was no outsider, nor was he self-taught. He was not working class
insights.locator: LS Lowry is not who you think

insights.claim: Lowry is claimed by politicians across the spectrum, from Margaret Thatcher to Andy Burnham, who calls him his favourite painter, as a chronicler of a northern English way of life the author calls more nostalgic than real.
insights.speaker: David McAllister
insights.so_what: Lowry functions as a cross-party symbol of northern English identity, useful context for cultural-political branding.

insights.claim: Lowry virtually never painted from life; he sketched while working as a rent collector and painted at home through the night, which explains the dreamlike, controlled unreality of his scenes.
insights.speaker: David McAllister
insights.so_what: Biographical detail underpinning the exhibition's reinterpretation.
insights.locator: Lowry would owe a lifelong debt

themes.theme: Formal template and the hidden eccentric

insights.claim: Most of Lowry's best-known landscapes follow a template of three horizontal bands with the horizon about two-thirds up or down and shallow perspective, relying on crowds to imply depth, making buildings look like stage props.
insights.speaker: David McAllister
insights.so_what: Analytical framework for reading Lowry's work.

insights.claim: Works like A Football Match (1932), unpeopled seascapes and grotesque portraiture show humour, camp melodrama and a refusal simply to give the public what it wanted.
insights.speaker: David McAllister
insights.so_what: Lesser-known Lowry genres may gain attention after the show.
insights.locator: But if this tells us a lot

insights.claim: The exhibition 'Lowry: The Theatre of Life' runs at MK Gallery, Milton Keynes, until 28 February, aiming to restore the eccentric behind the popular image.
insights.speaker: David McAllister
insights.so_what: Regional UK gallery programming as a draw for cultural tourism.
